title: Network Security Groups
description: Use network security groups to control traffic flowing into and out of Azure subnets and network interfaces.

data.text: A network security group, or NSG, is like a firewall rules list for your Azure resources. It contains security rules that allow or deny traffic based on source and destination, ports, and protocol. You can attach an NSG to a subnet or directly to a network interface.

Each NSG contains inbound and outbound rules. Every rule has a priority number, and Azure evaluates rules from lowest to highest. Once a rule matches, Azure stops checking further rules. This makes rule order very important.

data.title: NSG rule components
items: **Name**: A friendly label for the rule
**Source/Destination**: IP address, tag, or service tag
**Source/Destination port ranges**: Specific ports or ranges

data.text: Every NSG comes with default rules that Azure creates automatically. These defaults allow VNet-to-VNet traffic, load balancer health probes, and outbound internet access. You cannot remove default rules, but you can override them with higher-priority custom rules.

data.text: Application security groups, or ASGs, let you group virtual machines by application or function. Instead of writing rules with IP addresses, you reference an ASG. This is much easier to manage when servers are added or removed.

rows: Add VMs to an ASG instead

data.text: Service endpoints extend your VNet's private address space to Azure services. For example, you can enable the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on a subnet so traffic to Azure Storage stays on the Microsoft backbone network instead of going over the public internet.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: NSGs filter traffic with allow and deny rules.
Lower priority numbers are evaluated first.
ASGs simplify rules by grouping VMs by role.
Service endpoints keep traffic to Azure services on Microsoft's network.
data.takeaway: NSGs are your first line of defense for controlling Azure network traffic.
